fixes.explanation: Son, friend. The writer says Abraham was ready to offer his one and only son on the altar. This is the man who had received the promises, so the stakes couldn't be higher. I think this one hurts, so I'll say it once and let it sit.
Abraham was the one being tested here. The verse says he was ready to offer his one and only son, not a lamb. That son was Isaac, and I think that's what makes this verse so heavy.
The verse doesn't say servant, friend. Abraham was ready to offer his one and only son. God had said, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” That's why this test weighs so much.

That's how Abraham held it together, friend. The promise says Isaac and the test says Isaac, and he lands on this: “Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead…” The writer adds that in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.

True, friend. The writer says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. Then comes the line: “…in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.” Notice those words, 'in a sense.' I'll keep them right where the writer put them.

He worships. Jacob blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. He's dying, he's leaning on a staff, and he's still worshiping. I can barely get through a morning without leaning on the counter and complaining.

Weeping isn't in this verse, friend. It says Jacob worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. That's right after he blessed each of Joseph's sons. If you want tears, I'll supply them, because I get misty over a perfectly stamped cookie.

Esau shows up in verse 20, when Isaac blesses Jacob and Esau. He isn't in verse 21, though. There, Jacob blesses each of Joseph's sons and worships as he leans on the top of his staff. Different verse, different scene, friend.

That's it, friend. With his end near, Joseph spoke about the exodus of the Israelites. Most of us use our last words to ask where the good oven mitts went. This man is looking at the whole future of a people.
That's not what this verse says. Hebrews 11:22 says Joseph spoke about the exodus of the Israelites. He also gave instructions about his bones. Keep your eyes on the exodus, friend.
Close to the neighborhood but not the house, friend. Hebrews 11:22 says Joseph spoke about the exodus of the Israelites. It names no new king. The verse is looking ahead to Israel leaving.

It's the other way around, friend. The writer says Moses' parents hid him for three months, and “…they were unafraid of the king’s edict.” They saw that he was a beautiful child. Staying unafraid of a king's edict is more nerve than I have on a Monday.

Hebrews 11:25 says the reverse, friend. It says Moses “…chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin.” So he picked suffering with God's people. He took the hard seat over the comfy one that doesn't last.

False. The text says Moses “…chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin.” So he went with God's people, not with the enjoyment. That word 'fleeting' says it all, friend. He picked the hard seat with God's people over the comfy one that doesn't last.

A throne, friend? Nice guess, but nobody's handing out thrones in this verse. It says Moses valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, “…for he was looking ahead to his reward.” Reward is the word, and I'd hold onto it tighter than the last cookie in the box.

A palace? That's a lot of house to guess, friend. The verse sets disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt and never mentions a palace. What Moses was looking ahead to is his reward, and that's the word the writer picked.
That's the one. The writer says Moses “…persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.” That's what carried him when he left Egypt, not fearing the king's anger. Keep that line close, friend.
No cheering section in this verse, friend. The writer says Moses “…persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.” That's what the writer points to, not a crowd.

Dry, friend. The writer says by faith the people passed through the Red Sea “…as on dry land…” Think about that: a whole sea, and they crossed it as on dry land. That's a sentence worth reading twice.
Mud would be a rough walk, friend, but that's not what the writer says. He says the people passed through the Red Sea “…as on dry land…” No mud in this verse. The picture he gives is dry land.
The verse says the opposite, friend. Rahab, the prostitute, “…welcomed the spies in peace…” That's why she did not perish with those who were disobedient.
They shut the mouths of lions, friend. The writer lists it right alongside conquering kingdoms and administering justice. And all of it is through faith.
Chasing isn't in this verse, friend. It says these people of faith “…shut the mouths of lions…” Shutting mouths is the action the writer names, not chasing.
Fire, friend. The verse says they “…quenched the raging fire…” Then it adds that they escaped the edge of the sword. I get nervous when my oven runs a little hot, so I'm tipping my hat to them.
Flood isn't in this verse, friend. It says they “…quenched the raging fire…” and escaped the edge of the sword. The word here is fire.
A storm? Nice try, friend. The writer says they “…quenched the raging fire…” and escaped the edge of the sword. A storm would blow right past a bakery, but fire I take personally.

True, friend. The writer says these people of faith “…gained strength from weakness…” That line sits right between escaping the edge of the sword and becoming mighty in battle. Honestly, that gives me some hope.

The text says it's true, friend. The writer says these people of faith “…gained strength from weakness…” It's right there in verse 34, next to becoming mighty in battle. Weakness wasn't the end of the story for them.
The writer flips it, friend. He says, “The world was not worthy of them.” So the statement has it backwards. This comes right after the swords, the deserts and the caves and holes in the ground.
